sources.title: Anthropic mathematician claims to have solved prestigious Millennium Prize problem with Claude
sources.text: An Anthropic mathmetician’s latest breakthrough is another sign of how quickly AI is transforming mathematics. An Anthropic mathmetician’s latest breakthrough is another sign of how quickly AI is transforming mathematics. If you buy something from a link, The Verge may earn a commission. See our ethics statement. Anthropic mathematician Levent Alpöge claims he has proved the Riemann hypothesis, one of mathematics’s most notoriously difficult problems, with the help of Claude, cracking a puzzle that has eluded some of the world’s best mathematicians for decades. If verified, it would mark yet another seismic achievement for AI in mathematics and add to the upheaval already unleashed by OpenAI’s previous, often inelegant forays into the field. Alpöge’s solution has yet to be verified independently. Anthropic has not commented or involved itself in Alpöge’s announcement. In a document on his website , Alpöge says he texted Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei about the solution “late Sunday night” and suggests he held off publication until after the company’s IPO on Thursday . The Riemann hypothesis is one of seven Millennium Prize problems, which are widely considered some of the most formidable open challenges in mathematics. First proposed in 1859, the Riemann hypothesis concerns the distribution of prime numbers and how zeroes of a function are involved. It’s regarded as one of the most important unsolved problems in mathematics. A statement on Alpöge’s website says Claude was integral to developing the proof: I believe I have, working with Claude, discovered a proof 1 of the Riemann Hypothesis. In fact, the method easily extends much further, resolving the so-called Generalized Riemann Hypothesis, and I expect, with more time, the Extended Riemann Hypothesis too. Claude and I have also formalized the arguments without assumptions. It is natural to feel that this is an end, in my case a loss of a principal guiding light, but what I saw during the course of progress so amazed me that I believe it is one dawn across science of something far greater. The Verge reached out to Anthropic but didn’t immediately hear back. Anthropic said it was working on the Riemann Hypothesis with Claude in August , but noted at the time: “We don’t expect that the techniques Claude used will lead to proving the Riemann hypothesis.” Alpöge’s solution, presented in Lean, has only been published on his website and has not yet been publicly accepted by the Clay Mathematics Institute, which administers the Millennium Prize and offers a $1 million bounty for each problem solved. Under the institute’s rules , a proposed solution must be published and withstand at least two years of scrutiny before it can be considered for the prize, during which time it must have “received general acceptance in the global mathematics community.” In the quarter-century since the prize was established, only one problem has been officially solved: The Poincaré conjecture , a topological problem concerning three-dimensional spheres. In September, OpenAI claimed to have cracked another, the Navier-Stokes problem, which concerns the flow of fluids. OpenAI said it pursued Navier-Stokes after hearing rumors that rival researchers were closing in on a solution. Alpöge had been working on the problem with New York University mathematics professor Tristan Buckmaster. Buckmaster claimed OpenAI produced a solution for Navier-Stokes using the route he and Alpöge were working on with OpenAI’s Codex and Claude. OpenAI spent millions of dollars and deployed 10,000 agents in the attempt. The result is widely considered credible, though it has yet to receive formal recognition. But the achievement has been marred by allegations of questionable research practices, including claims it used unpublished work from mathematicians who had shared their research with its AI tools. OpenAI has strongly denied wrongdoing, but this has done little to quell the uproar. Though most of the spotlight has been on OpenAI’s movement in math, Alpöge said in July that he solved the Jacobean conjecture using Claude. The deluge of findings has left mathematicians scrambling to digest the material and figure out where they belong in what is rapidly becoming a profoundly different mathematical landscape.

sources.title: Anthropic researcher claims to have proven Riemann hypothesis using Claude
sources.text: An Anthropic PBC researcher claims to have used Claude to prove the Riemann hypothesis, which is widely considered to be the most important open question in mathematics. Levent Alpöge announced his discovery today on his personal website. Anthropic has not published an official announcement about the news. The company floated on the Nasdaq a day earlier in a landmark public offering that raised over $93 billion. “I believe I have, working with Claude, discovered a proof of the Riemann hypothesis,” Alpöge wrote in a four-page statement. “What I saw during the course of progress so amazed me that I believe it is one dawn across science of something far greater.” The Riemann hypothesis was proposed in the mid-1800s by its namesake, the mathematician Bernhard Riemann. It focuses on a specific mathematical function, the Riemann zeta function, that was discovered more than a century earlier. A function is similar to a software program: It takes a piece of data as input and outputs another piece of data. A function’s input and output can be numbers, other functions and many other mathematical objects. The Riemann zeta function’s input and output are both complex numbers. Complex numbers share similarities with regular numbers, but also have many additional properties. When the inputs and outputs of the Riemann zeta function are visualized, they resemble a three-dimensional spiral. The Riemann hypothesis is concerned with a specific section of that 3D spiral. In that section, the complex numbers outputted by the Riemann zeta function all equal zero. The hypothesis argues that the inputs from which those outputs are derived all include the value ½. The hypothesis is considered to be the most important open problem in mathematics for multiple reasons. The first is that although it focuses on a single, not overly complicated mathematical function, its implications extend to a far bigger topic: prime numbers. If the Riemann hypothesis is correct, a seemingly random aspect of prime numbers is in fact regulated by a pattern. Another factor behind the hypothesis’ importance is that hundreds of theorems operate on the assumption that it’s true. If the Riemann hypothesis is correct, those theorems are correct as well. Alpöge wrote that Claude proved not only the standard version of the Riemann hypothesis but also the so-called generalized variant. The latter conjecture argues that the Riemann hypothesis holds true for not only the Riemann zeta function but also certain other, similar functions. Alpöge believes that Claude will be capable of proving an even broader version of the hypothesis in the future. The researcher detailed that Claude’s proof runs for more than 250,000 pages. He has not yet released the paper. He did, however, publish a version of the proof written in Lean, a programming language used to verify mathematical results. The file contains millions of lines of code. Proofs implemented in Lean are essentially regular software programs. If a Lean program runs without crashing, the mathematical argument that it describes is correct. That makes it easier for mathematicians to verify newly published proofs. sources.title: Anthropic employee claims to have proven the most famous math problem using Claude
sources.text: Levent Alpöge says he worked with Claude to discover a proof of the Riemann Hypothesis. A mathematician working for Anthropic claims to have discovered a proof of the Riemann Hypothesis using Claude. According to the BBC , Levent Alpöge used Claude to create a detailed proof of the problem over the course of six weeks. "This problem has been the sacred object in mathematics for me since my childhood," Alpöge said in his announcement . In very simple terms, Bernhard Riemann proposed way back in 1859 that prime numbers' locations along the number line have a meaningful order. Prime numbers are whole numbers that cannot be divided by anything other than themselves and the number one, if you want them to produce another whole number. As Scientific American notes, the Riemann Hypothesis is often considered the most important unsolved problem in math. The Clay Mathematics Institute recognizes it as one of its Millennium Prize Problems and had promised $1 million to the one who can find the first correct solution for it. Alpöge has presented his findings in a programming language called Lean that can be used to write and confirm mathematical proofs. He said the complete proof is over 250,000 pages long. In October, OpenAI also posted hundreds of solutions to previously unsolved math problems, as well as progress towards some of them, including the Riemann Hypothesis. It could take some time to confirm those solutions, just as it could take time to confirm Alpöge's Claude proof. James Maynard, a University of Oxford in England mathematician, told The New York Times he was "98 or 99 percent certain" that Alpöge's discovery is accurate. If it is, then Anthropic's AI has solved a 167-year-old problem that even the world's brightest minds couldn't.

stories.title: Tech wreck drags Anthropic into the red on its second day of trading
stories.summary: Nasdaq futures trade lower after steep declines extend across global tech stocks

sources.name: CNBC Technology
sources.title: Tech wreck drags Anthropic into the red on its second day of trading
sources.text: This is CNBC's Morning Squawk newsletter. Subscribe here to receive future editions in your inbox. Hello, this is Leonie Kidd with today's edition of Morning Squawk. Despite its debut-day rally, the broader markets plunged around the stock, and it's now catching the tech cold - down in premarket trading on its second day as a public company. It's day 2 and Anthropic shares are under pressure. The stock is falling in premarket trading , at one point down over 6%. The stock had closed 17% higher in its first day of trading, easing back from a near-40% jump earlier in the session. Speaking exclusively to CNBC's Andrew Ross Sorkin after ringing the bell at the Nasdaq, CEO Dario Amodei defended the company's massive $900 billion in AI commitments, saying, "If you look at the amount of cash we have on the balance sheet and the amount of revenue that we're already making per year, suddenly those commitments don't seem so large." Nasdaq futures are back in the red, underperforming both the Dow and S&P in early trading. Nvidia is lower in premarket trading, alongside AMD . It's a deeply negative handover from Asia and Europe. Japan's Softbank suffered its worst trading day in over two years as the AI sell-off swept through the Asian tech sector. Shares in CXMT , SK Hynix and others ended the day deep in the red. In Europe, chip stocks like ASML , Infineon and others suffered heavy selling. The debate over the export of U.S.-made chips to China has divided the Trump Administration's cabinet. The Nvidia scandal has further exposed this split and fanned the flames between the two camps. CNBC's Morning Squawk recaps the biggest stories investors should know before the stock market opens, every weekday morning. Bitcoin hit a 4-month low amid the broader tech sell-off, putting further pressure on cryptocurrencies . Precious metals investors can be forgiven if they feel like the past year has given them whiplash. Following a torrid run in which the price of gold hit new records 53 times in 2025, it hit a historic high of $5,589.38 an ounce on Jan. 28, only to take an almost equally historic nosedive. On Wednesday, gold fell below $3,800 for the first time since September 2025, roughly a third below its peak. A convergence of factors pushed gold to historic highs earlier this year, according to Suki Cooper, global head of commodities research at Standard Chartered, the London-based multinational bank. Now a different convergence is bringing the price down. — CNBC's Alexa LoMonaco, Shikhar Gupta, Vanna Ben'Ous, Daren Fonda, Chloe Taylor, Luke Fountain, and Kevin Williams contributed to this report.

sources.name: The Guardian Technology
sources.title: Nasdaq erases all 2026 gains as AI sell-off dampens Anthropic’s second day of trading
sources.text: The Nasdaq lost trillions in value, with the AI startup’s IPO failing to buoy it as investors question huge sums being poured into AI buildout Who are Anthropic’s seven co-founders, now worth $180bn? As Anthropic’s stock dropped during its second day of trading, the wider stock market dipped with it. On Friday, the Nasdaq Composite erased all its gains for 2026 and closed down 5% from its value on 1 January. The Dow Jones Industrial Average and S&P 500 closed in correction territory. Anthropic’s record-breaking IPO failed to stem a global sell-off in AI-linked companies, and the tech-heavy Nasdaq erased some $4tn in market value this week, according to the Wall Street Journal. Shares in the frontier AI company behind the Claude chatbot, which floated in the US on Thursday, fell by 9% on Friday, ceding most of the gains from the biggest initial public offering in history. They dropped to $88.30, towards the $83 level at which Anthropic priced its stock market debut. Anthropic’s first two days as a listed company have been volatile. Its shares jumped by 17% on Thursday, after briefly surging by almost 40% when trading in the firm began. US technology stocks followed Anthropic down on Friday, with the memory chipmaker SanDisk falling 14% and rival Micron down 12%. Nvidia fell 14%, eliminating hundreds of billions of dollars in market cap. Neil Wilson, a UK investor strategist at Saxo, said there was “just relentless selling in tech”. He warned: “Anthropic shares tumbled to take an $85 handle as the post-IPO euphoria gives way to the reality of a steep sell-off across the tech and AI space that shows no sign of easing just yet.” Global markets slumped on Friday too; Asian stock markets recorded their worst week since 2020, as shares in big chip companies fell. In Taiwan, stocks dropped 6.7% to hit their lowest point since mid-April, with the chip maker TSMC down about 6%. The scale of the decline in Taiwan prompted the chair of its stock exchange to pledge to ensure the stable operation ⁠of capital markets, and reassure investors they should remain confident in the fundamentals of Taiwanese companies. In Japan, the Nikkei index fell 5%, while South Korea’s tech-heavy Kospi index lost 5.5%. Shares in the tech investor SoftBank had their worst day in more than two years, down 14.5% in Tokyo, amid worries around its aggressive bets on AI. European stock markets posted their biggest weekly loss since March 2025, with the pan-European Stoxx 600 dropping 1.9% on Friday. London’s blue-chip stock index hit a five-month low. The sell-off followed losses on Wall Street on Thursday, where the main indices all fell by more than 2% on a day dominated by Anthropic’s IPO . Chris Beauchamp, the chief market analyst at the investing and trading platform IG, said Anthropic could be “draining market liquidity”, as investors sell shares in other companies to raise funds to pay for stock in the newly floated AI firm. “The slide from yesterday’s highs sends a message that there might be more at work here than investors realise, and while brokers are scrambling to buy more, that liquidity has to come from somewhere, and the other tech names may be the first ones to feel the pressure,” Beauchamp said. Anthropic’s flotation has failed to ease worries around the AI trade, as investors increasingly question whether companies can deliver the returns necessary to justify the billions of dollars being poured into the AI buildout. Daniela Hathorn, a senior market analyst at Capital.com, said: “The IPO demonstrated that demand for AI exposure remains strong, but it has not been enough to overcome concerns about elevated valuations, profitability and the sustainability of investment spending. “The broader market mood has shifted from buying the dip towards questioning whether the correction has further to run. The weakness in equal-weighted indices suggests that selling pressure is no longer confined to a handful of technology giants, while Europe’s recent outperformance has also faded.” Nvidia shares fell byafter California served the chip company with a subpoena as part of an investigation into whether its advanced semiconductors ended up in China. Britain’s FTSE 100 share index dropped by 5.1% this week, its biggest weekly fall since the start of the Iran war. Fears that US central bankers may raise interest rates to fight inflation have lifted the dollar to a 19-month high, and pushed down the gold price – with gold on track for its worst week since March. Bitcoin hit its lowest level in four months, dropping below the $60,000 point for the first time since early July.

sources.name: The Guardian Technology
sources.title: ‘The greatest game ever made’: readers and Guardian staff on Grand Theft Auto VI
sources.text: Rockstar’s newest installment of its hit franchise still has plenty of action, along with a dose of ‘healthy masculinity’ D escribed as the biggest entertainment launch in history, the new Grand Theft Auto game has prompted avid fans around the world to take the day off work, stock up on snacks and celebrate its arrival after 13 years of waiting. While some have already spent hours immersed in the game’s criminal escapades, others have found themselves doing household chores, building houses or simply taking in the scenery – which includes more than 170 flora and fauna species native to Florida . GTA VI has generated extraordinary global anticipation for its action-packed gameplay, but players are now finding new delight in the game’s more intimate moments. From the relationship between protagonists Jason and Lucia to the painstaking world-building of Leonida, Rockstar’s fictional take on Florida, players have shared their wide-ranging experiences with the Guardian, revealing what has surprised and challenged them about this long-awaited release – and what this all means for the series’ evolution. Pete Langhelt, 39, from Colchester, pre-ordered GTA VI “as soon as I could”, and has been looking forward to its release for a long time. “Out of my group of friends I’m probably the only one really nerding out about it,” he says. While Pete hasn’t been able to take time from work in the civil service, he’s still clocked “about 10 hours” of gameplay already. “The core of the missions themselves are pretty similar,” he says. “You turn up somewhere, shoot a load of people and escape. But the development of the characters has changed an awful lot. I have enjoyed the dynamic between Jason and Lucia. I never thought you could make comfortable domesticity into an enjoyable side activity in a video game.” Pete has played all the installments of GTA franchise from the first, when he was “probably too young to be playing”. “I think Red Dead Redemption 2 was my favourite Rockstar game going into this, and it seems to have developed the things that I really liked about Red Dead.” The game encourages exploration, he says. “The day and night cycle seems a lot less intense than GTA V, meaning you don’t feel rushed to get things done. I can let Jason take a slow start to the day before taking a slow drive or boat ride to whatever criminal activity needs completing.” His partner is less keen. “She’ll have to put up with me being on the Xbox for the next few weeks,” he says. A 59-year-old MBA retiree from Venice, Florida, was also struck by just how much of the experience revolves around everyday life. He described it as the “most beautiful, real, open-world game that’s ever existed”. “I was surprised that, with about 10-plus hours of play, most of my time has been spent performing mundane tasks like home repair, grocery shopping, personal grooming and trying to open a bank account. The realism is incredible, but perhaps too real,” he said. “It’s as fully realized as a game world could be. I never expected to see anything more fully developed,” he added. Rob Smeraldo, 28, from Dundee, took the day off work yesterday to play the game on his PlayStation 5. “I made sure I had loads of snacks and Domino’s,” he says. And already, Rob believes that “GTA VI must be the greatest game ever made”. “I think the realism and just the detail put into it is absolutely astounding. The shadows, the way the hair moves when people move around … They took their time, but it’s definitely been worth it,” he says. Rob is a longtime GTA fan and wore a GTA VI T-shirt and drank from a GTA mug to mark the occasion. “I purchased the physical copy [of the game] as soon as it became purchasable – I just wanted the memorabilia, you know?” Ella Delancey, 35, of Berkshire has been playing GTA since she was a child. “GTA III is a huge core memory for me. My brother and I were much too young to be playing it and I definitely wouldn’t let my daughter play it now, but at the time we were obsessed.” So far, the social and brand director has been surprised by how much there is to do aside from pushing the story forward. “I’m not very far into it yet, but I’m already struck by the graphics and the sheer depth of what you can do. It’s very violent, obviously, but I play by the rules, which probably makes me a bit boring. I’ve been birdwatching and exploring, and there’s so much to do outside the main story.” There is one thing she is struggling with, however, and that’s Lucia, one of the main protagonists, leaving her child in a cafe and going to prison, only to come out and start committing more crimes. “As a mother, that doesn’t sit comfortably with me. I know it’s a game and you have to suspend your morals to a degree, but that part has given me pause,” she says. “I do think it’s a step forward that you can no longer hire sex workers as in previous games. GTA still has a complicated relationship with misogyny – and it’s far from perfect, but that change feels significant.” While Ella hasn’t taken any time off work to play, she has set aside time on Friday to play or watch her partner play. “It’s so immersive that it doesn’t feel like a chore, and I can see it replacing our usual after-work TV downtime for a little while,” she says. Clint, 36, who works in the music industry in Chicago, describes the game as “truly one of one”, pointing to its unexpectedly domestic moments and the relationship between Jason and Lucia as some of its biggest draws. “The story is just downright cute. I just had my character build an Ikea table with his girlfriend, and loved it. I typically skip some cutscenes, but now I’m rewatching them when I miss something,” he says. sources.title: ¿Qué ha perdido ‘GTA 6’ comparado con los Grand Theft Auto anteriores?
sources.text: El hype por GTA 6 ha pagado con creces. Lo nuevo de Rockstar Games debutó en los últimos días con una respuesta inmejorable tanto del público como de la crítica especializada. La espera de 13 años para tener un nuevo Grand Theft Auto ha valido la pena, aunque a los jugadores también les ha llamado la atención la ausencia de algunas características de sus predecesores . Algunas de estas omisiones tienen una explicación totalmente narrativa, mientras que otras responden a una decisión práctica por parte de los desarrolladores. Está claro que GTA 6 es una propuesta con cada detalle cuidado al extremo y que apunta a brindar la experiencia más inmersiva (y realista) en la historia de la saga. Esto también implica que han tenido que enfocarse en la imagen grande y hacer algunas concesiones en beneficio de la historia que plantea GTA 6 . El caso más notorio es que ya no puedes contratar prostitutas , algo que ya formaba parte del ADN de la franquicia. Pero ojo, que esto no responde a que en Rockstar se hayan vuelto mojigatos o les carcoma la conciencia . Desde la compañía explicaron a ShackNews que quitaron dicha función para resaltar el componente crucial del juego, que es la evolución del vínculo entre Jason y Lucía. “ GTA VI es un juego sobre una pareja en una situación complicada: amantes a la fuga. Si bien hemos conservado muchos elementos de entregas anteriores de GTA , todo lo que hemos implementado en esta sexta entrega responde al espíritu de la historia que queríamos contar y a los sistemas de juego que deseábamos ampliar, tales como el sistema de búsqueda policial, la radio, los atracos y el robo de vehículos. Aunque muchos aspectos de títulos anteriores no están presentes en GTA VI , consideramos que los elementos que hemos incluido son necesarios y complementarios para transmitir las sensaciones y motivaciones que queríamos destacar a lo largo de la historia de Jason y Lucía”. Esto no quiere decir que los jugadores estén obligados a cultivar la relación romántica entre Jason y Lucía. GTA 6 les da la libertad a los jugadores de decidir si quieren que los protagonistas sigan juntos o si prefieren que rompan . No obstante, el hilo conductor que se presenta desde el comienzo incluye un objetivo en común que excede a los protagonistas. Así, incluir la opción de contratar prostitutas parece algo innecesario y descartable . Es cierto que las primeras horas de GTA 6 tienen un poco de girlfriend simulator , pero también es una realidad que transitar ese camino paga con creces cuando las cosas dan un giro para lo peor. Sin meternos en spoilers, hay un punto de quiebre en la misión para trabajar con Mattia que pone todo en su lugar. Pero mucho antes de llegar a esa parte, ni recordarás que el juego no te permite contratar prostitutas y matarlas para recuperar tu dinero. GTA 6 está plagado de minijuegos y actividades complementarias. Sin embargo, los jugadores han notado que falta uno que ya era un clásico de la saga Grand Theft Auto y de GTA Online . Nos referimos, claro, a los dardos . Pero no es el único ausente, pues lo nuevo de Rockstar Games tampoco permite jugar a los bolos . Rockstar también ha dado una explicación sobre esto. La firma prefirió dejar de lado algunos minijuegos en GTA 6 porque ya no había tiempo para hacerlos como correspondía . Estas actividades sirven como una extensión de las físicas del juego, algo que se puede ver en las partidas de pool en The Rusty Anchor, y desarrollarlas como correspondía habría demandado una carga todavía mayor sobre el equipo. Después de todo, cada minijuego es un videojuego con vida propia dentro de otro videojuego. “El caso de los dardos es polémico. A veces se oye decir que hay dinero o tiempo ilimitados, pero ni siquiera nosotros disponemos de ello. Por eso, a veces hay que reconocer que no vamos a ser capaces de alcanzar el nivel que consideramos necesario”, explicó Rob Nelson, uno de los jefes de Rockstar North, a VGC .
